vignette:
Mereana had been born in the Pacific Islands and had built a careful life in the United States with her husband, working for years as an auditor, the sort of job that had once suited her need for order and precision. During the war, when she was a civilian trying to get through an ordinary day in an unfamiliar place, that order was shattered in a moment she still could not put into words. She could describe the facts if pressed, but the event itself remained strangely wordless to her: she knew what happened, yet when she tried to tell it, the details seemed to stall in her throat. What stayed with her most vividly were fragments that came as if printed on paper and laid out before her. She would see the scene in her mind like a series of photographs, each one fixed and unblinking, and certain smells would return with them so sharply that she felt taken back into that place. The scent of sweat or body odour, even years later, could bring the whole moment rushing close again, as if the air around her had changed and the room she was in was no longer the room she was in.

In the months and years that followed, Mereana began to notice that certain ordinary moments could pull her back into that experience without warning. If she was feeling happy or relaxed, perhaps sitting with her husband after dinner or enjoying a quiet afternoon, she would suddenly become uneasy, almost suspicious of the calm itself, as though letting herself settle made her vulnerable to what might come next. At work, the workplace that had once given her structure became a place she approached with more vigilance. She watched the room as soon as she entered, taking note of where she could sit so that her back would be against a wall and she could see everyone else. She felt unsafe unless she had that position, and if she could not arrange it, she remained distracted, aware of exits, doorways, and the possibility of someone coming up behind her. She also found herself frequently looking behind her to check whether someone might be following her, a habit that had spread beyond the office into parking lots, hallways, and any place where she could not easily account for every person around her.

Mereana had come to spend a great deal of time trying to make sense of the event, turning it over in her mind in ways that never resolved anything. She rehearsed what she might say before any interaction, sometimes even before a brief conversation with a colleague or a clerk, as though preparing every line could protect her from being caught off guard. At night, she went back over how the event could have been prevented, asking herself what she might have done differently, and then circling through the question of why it had happened to her in particular. These thoughts did not bring comfort; they simply filled the quiet hours and left her more tired, more preoccupied, and less able to settle into the life around her.

What distressed Mereana deeply was the sense that the event had marked her in a way others could somehow see. She felt that people could look at her and know what had happened, as if it were written on her face or in the way she carried herself. That belief made her guarded in public and self-conscious in relationships, even with people she trusted. She feared that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, as though something essential had been lost during the war and could not be recovered. At times she also found herself thinking that her life was not worth living anymore, not in a dramatic or impulsive way, but as a bleak, weary conclusion that surfaced when she felt most overwhelmed by the constancy of these memories and the effort of keeping herself composed.

Although she continued to work, she did so with increasing strain, managing her duties while monitoring the room, her body, and the people near her. She had become more careful in social situations, more deliberate in what she said, and more exhausted by the effort of appearing unaffected. What finally brought Mereana to seek help was the growing weight of these experiences and her wish not to keep living as though danger were always near. She came hoping for some relief from the images, the smells, the constant checking, and the sense of being visibly changed, but what she feared most was that she might never feel safe, normal, or fully herself again.
